# Only 36% of companies prioritize gender equality in their corporate strategy

**This is revealed in the document "** _**Gender Equity in Colombian Companies: Analysis of Sustainability Reports and Trends 2025**_ **," prepared by the EAFIT Center for Management and Business, which evaluated the 115 largest companies in the country, 43% of which have a sustainability report.**

**Among**

**the findings, it is highlighted that companies with greater female participation report better financial results. Furthermore, sectors such as mining and agriculture have the lowest female representation in the workforce, with figures of 26% and 29%, respectively.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [EAFIT is in the News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/eafit-es-noticia)
- Only 36% of companies prioritize gender equality in their corporate strategy

![Image: Only 36% of companies prioritize gender equality in their corporate strategy](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/e16c3fc2-7740-4daf-a670-cfddb71528eb/web/informe-equidad-genero-2025.jpeg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=qG9raf1o)

Gender equality in the business world remains a central issue on the sustainability and competitiveness agenda of Colombian companies. An analysis conducted by EAFIT University's Center for Management and Business on the 115 companies with the highest operating incomes across various sectors reveals progress in the inclusion of women in the workforce, but also shows that challenges persist in terms of leadership, pay equity, and training. Although 43% of the companies analyzed have a publicly available or easily accessible sustainability report, only 36% prioritize gender equality as a critical issue within their corporate strategy.

“We are currently experiencing a setback, induced by the policies the United States has adopted regarding diversity and inclusion. Therefore, this report is timely, as it will likely provide tools for moving forward. One of the trends we will observe is that the discussion on diversity and inclusion will shift towards a conversation more focused on the market and business than on social responsibility. This report, in a way, is a tool for those who choose that path,” explains Cristina Vélez Valencia, Dean of the EAFIT School of Management and co-author of the document, which was developed over nearly a year.

One of the most significant findings is the relationship between gender equality and financial performance. Companies with greater female participation in their workforce tend to report better financial results; however, this trend does not necessarily translate into equitable access to leadership positions. Despite progress in workplace inclusion, women continue to be underrepresented in management positions and on executive committees, which limits their influence on strategic decision-making.

Another finding of the report shows that the gender gap varies significantly across sectors. While commerce and services have higher female participation, at 50% and 37% respectively, sectors such as mining and agriculture show the lowest levels, at just 26% and 29%. This disparity demonstrates that certain work environments still present structural barriers that hinder women's inclusion.

A critical factor identified in the analysis is inequality in training and professional development. In most sectors, women receive fewer training hours than men, which impacts their advancement within organizations. This disparity is particularly pronounced in sectors such as mining and construction, where training opportunities for women remain limited.

Among the challenges identified, the retention of female talent stands out. While women have lower turnover rates in some sectors, in others, such as manufacturing, their turnover is significantly higher than that of men (25.06% women vs. 8.55% men). This suggests that many still face barriers to remaining in their jobs or advancing within their organizations.

The gender pay gap remains a reality in the Colombian business sector. In 2021, according to the National Administrative Department of Statistics (DANE), women in Colombia earned 6.3% less than men on average, with the greatest disparities observed among groups with lower levels of education, in rural areas, among widows, and among marginalized ethnic groups. Despite the existence of regulations mandating equal pay, only a fraction of companies transparently report this data in their sustainability reports.

Alexa Barco López, a researcher at the Center for Management and Business and also an author of the report, explains that several challenges arose during the document's preparation, including information availability, a lack of standardized indicators, and the presence of some companies in different countries, which necessitated searching for data specific to Colombia. In her view, the findings are highly valuable.

“The idea is that, based on robust, data-driven research, trends and useful information will be generated for business leaders, enabling them to make better decisions, share sustainability recommendations, and identify opportunities for improvement. This will help close gaps on key issues for the world in general and for achieving the SDGs,” the researcher concludes.

###### Trends 2025

El informe​ identifica tendencias clave que marcarán el futuro de la equidad de género en las empresas colombianas durante 2025. Una de ellas es que solo las organizaciones que han integrado la Diversidad, Equidad e Inclusión (DEI) en su estrategia corporativa continuarán fortaleciendo estos esfuerzos. Muchas compañías que adoptaron políticas de equidad como una respuesta superficial a presiones externas podrían reducir o abandonar sus iniciativas, especialmente tras los recientes cambios en regulaciones internacionales y el debate global sobre la efectividad de estas políticas.

Otra tendencia es el giro de la conversación sobre DEI hacia un enfoque de negocio. Las empresas ya no solo justificarán sus políticas de equidad por razones éticas o de cumplimiento, sino que deberán demostrar su impacto en la rentabilidad y el desempeño organizacional. Los inversionistas y grupos de interés exigirán mayor evidencia económica que respalde la importancia de la equidad de género, lo que podría llevar a una discusión más profunda y con indicadores sobre su relevancia empresarial.

“La discusión se va a sofisticar. A quienes presenten reportes de diversidad, equidad e inclusión no se les pedirá únicamente que cuenten cuántas personas tienen, sino que realmente demuestren cómo esto está impactando su negocio. Vamos a ver una profundización en el análisis”, afirma la decana Cristina.

Finalmente, se espera una mayor cautela en la divulgación de avances en equidad de género. Algunas empresas, ante el contexto político y regulatorio global, podrían optar por reducir la visibilidad de sus iniciativas en informes de sostenibilidad, afectando la transparencia en la medición de progresos. Igualmente, la presión de inversionistas y organismos internacionales seguirá impulsando la inclusión de estos temas en la agenda corporativa, aunque con enfoques más estratégicos y alineados con los riesgos financieros y operativos de cada organización.
